Pregnancy

Lower abdominal pain when walking during pregnancy

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A pulling sensation, pelvic ache or cramp during a walk can be unsettling. Some causes relate to the changing support around the uterus or pelvis, while others need medical attention. The location, persistence and accompanying symptoms are more useful than simply labelling all walking-related pain “normal.”

Pause rather than pushing through pain

Stop the activity and rest in a comfortable position. Notice where the pain is, whether it comes in waves, how long it lasts and whether there are other symptoms.

If abdominal pain is new, recurs during exercise or does not settle, contact your maternity professional before resuming the activity. Pain improving with rest is helpful information, but does not rule out every important cause.

Do not feel obliged to finish a planned route or reach an exercise target. If you feel faint or unwell, get help rather than trying to walk home alone.

Common possibilities include ligament and pelvic pain

The ligaments supporting the growing uterus can cause a brief pulling or sharp discomfort, sometimes on one side. Constipation or trapped wind can also contribute to abdominal discomfort.

Pelvic girdle pain is often felt around the pubic area, groin, hips or lower back. Walking, stairs, standing on one leg or turning in bed may make it worse. It can be very painful without meaning that the baby is being harmed.

A clinician or pregnancy physiotherapist can help distinguish these patterns and advise on activity. Persistent pain should not be dismissed as something you simply have to tolerate until birth.

Urinary infection and pregnancy complications can also cause lower abdominal pain. A symptom appearing during a walk does not prove that walking caused it.

Know the symptoms that need urgent assessment

Contact the maternity unit or early-pregnancy service immediately for pain with vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, regular cramps or tightenings, or a change in the baby’s usual movements.

Pain with fever, painful urination, persistent vomiting or feeling generally unwell also needs prompt advice. Severe pain or pain that continues despite rest should be assessed.

Severe one-sided pain with shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or fainting in early pregnancy can signal an ectopic pregnancy. Call emergency services for collapse, severe pain with faintness, heavy bleeding, chest pain or major difficulty breathing.

A painful swollen calf needs urgent assessment for a possible blood clot. Do not massage it or continue exercising to see whether it improves.

Tell the clinician how many weeks pregnant you are and exactly what happened. The right service may differ in early and later pregnancy.

Walking is usually beneficial in an uncomplicated pregnancy

Regular moderate activity can support fitness, mood and metabolic health. For uncomplicated pregnancies, guidance commonly recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity across the week.

That might be spread across five 30-minute sessions or shorter manageable periods. It is a flexible target, not a requirement to exercise through pain or illness.

If you were inactive before pregnancy, build up gradually. A pace at which you can still talk is a practical guide to moderate effort. Some medical or obstetric conditions require an individualized plan.

Ordinary appropriate exercise has not been shown to increase miscarriage or preterm-birth risk in a healthy uncomplicated pregnancy. Having a pain episode does not mean you have harmed the baby by walking.

Regular pregnancy activity can help constipation, cardiovascular fitness and healthy weight gain, and may reduce the chance of gestational diabetes, hypertensive complications and caesarean birth. These are potential population benefits, not guarantees or a reason to ignore an individual restriction. Walking also has practical advantages: little equipment is needed, and short outings can fit into daily life.

Make activity more comfortable after assessment

Choose well-fitting, supportive shoes; flat supportive shoes can be appropriate. Avoid unstable footwear and routes with a high risk of falling.

Keep water available, avoid overheating and choose a comfortable pace. If pelvic pain is diagnosed, shorter strides, shorter walks or a different activity may be easier. A physiotherapist can advise whether a support belt or specific exercises may help.

Keep a note of activities that trigger symptoms and what relieves them. Share that information at follow-up so the plan can be adjusted.

The aim is to stay as comfortably active as your circumstances allow, with clear instructions about symptoms that mean stopping or seeking help.

If you are starting from little activity, five minutes can be a manageable first outing, with small increases as tolerated. Adding five minutes every week is one possible approach, not a compulsory schedule. Drink before and after activity as needed, use a level route and allow breaks before exhaustion. A comfortable supported flat shoe can work well.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

ACOG supports at least 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly for uncomplicated pregnancies, adjusted for symptoms and medical circumstances.

Abdominal pain or exercise warning symptoms require stopping and assessment rather than pushing through a target.

How BeMama can help

Choose a manageable route, supportive footwear and a pace that allows conversation, then adjust the plan with your care team if pain recurs.

When to seek help

Bleeding, fluid leakage, regular contractions, changed movements or persistent pain needs immediate maternity advice; collapse, chest pain or major breathlessness needs emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Stop and assess new pain instead of walking through it.
  • Bleeding, fluid leakage, severe pain or changed movements need prompt care.
  • A tailored activity plan can help preserve movement without ignoring symptoms.

Frequently asked questions

Does this mean walking caused a miscarriage risk?

Not necessarily. Appropriate exercise in an uncomplicated pregnancy is generally safe; the pain itself still deserves assessment when new, persistent or accompanied by warning signs.

Are flat shoes unsuitable?

No. Well-fitting flat shoes with good support are often appropriate. Comfort and stability matter more than a blanket rule about heel height.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
